asked camille to put this on at 10pm knowing i’d fall asleep and because i wanted to be put to sleep after a weird night emotionally (and there’s no writer who lulls me into somnambulatory hazes more than sorkin, see my myriad attempts to watch the social network that see me snoozing before garfield even gets to say the line about his prada being at the cleaners) and it worked, though i strangely was able to stay awake until damn near an hour twenty with this one and between that and the tens of clips of this i’ve seen during some time-wasting endeavor or another on short-form video applications in the last five+ years i think i’ve metabolized a percentage of the meaningful content of this film that’d be tantamount to a high-A letter-grade. in dearborn, michigan there’s a horrific acres-sprawling henry ford vanity project/oversized and undercontexted memorial, where ford himself picked up and moved edison’s actual lab/residence among other architectural objects important to the late-19th–early-20th centuries’ histories (which despite its obvious odiousness is at least appreciable in the way it’s essentially a super-sized and un-concealed in its greed version of the pillaging drive of all first-world museums, the bareness of it heightening these innate contradictions in a way that’s at least interesting to think about) assumedly as a way of creating a huge synecdoche of america that southeast michigan soon-to-be factory worker children could free roam around and think about the majesty of american ingenuity and invention. during the baseball season there were weekly games where crashed-out/aging minor league players would play baseball as close as possible to how it was played in the 1800s (for the record there were some black players who participated in this but don’t think it’s lost on me or likely the players that this was the specific time period they were tasked to replicate). my dad has a distant but oft-professed love of baseball, and would take our family to sit on the grass on the hill near third-base and eat cold sandwiches and cape cod potato chips and drink izzes sometimes in the summers, an activity that none of us enjoyed or got much out of except him. and while we were sitting there he’d get romantic about baseball as this monument to american cynicism and rugged-if-not-horrific individualism/single-mindedness, how it’s great because most of the gamesmanship happens off the field (either through direct cheating a la the world series fix gatsby is implicated in or the indirect underhanded tactics on display in this movie) but that ultimately it is a game played in real time with so many uncontrolled variables so as to make the thing always feel very alive despite its conceits. i think these descriptions are a lot of the reason i came to love racing so much in my adulthood, the vast team-wide conspiracies required to pull-off certain tech violations (see jeremy clarkson’s tale of lancia tricking fia officials into thinking they’d homologated twice as many 037s as they did , a story that always struck me as a real john hanley classic) or the way that back in the 80s team principles would run any fuel with any additive so long as it made the car faster even if it made the flames invisible as pit-crew-members burned to death. as vulgar and horrific as that level of avarice can be to witness, there’s something i love and find difficult to look away from in all of it. but it should be noted from the eras of sport my dad and now i show interest in that neither of the aforementioned activities really function like that anymore, or at least the stakes are lower and more controlled, and this stakeslessness is why i think my dad found it difficult to care about the period of baseball described in moneyball and why i find it hard to care about hamilton joining ferrari (next season guys i promise). sorkin does an okay job at filling this movie with chewy people-in-rooms dialogue and the director coaxes some decent performances from pitt, hoffman and hill, and sorkin at least has similar thoughts about the game as my dad in a way that made me feel tenderly enough to write this very long review about a movie i was asleep for part of, but he seldom-if-ever works to illustrate why baseball is still a game worthy of keeping his or my father’s rapt attention and in that failure this movie ends up pretty dead on arrival, dead especially because if anyone could be convinced the conniving magic is still there in sport it’s me. but hey, fun movie to fall asleep to and it’s one of the few movies recently that really made me want to have kids without the kid in question being a literal infant–toddler, so it wasn’t for nothing.

"Sabermetrics" is the application of statistical analysis to baseball records, esp. in order to evaluate and compare the performance of individual players. The definition alone puts most people to sleep, and yet they made a movie about it. So if you haven't watch any of the trailers and don't know anything about it, Moneyball is the true story of Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), the manager of the Oakland A's who used the sabermetrics concept to stay within his ghetto Oakland budget in order to get a decent team. All the good players like Jason Giambi and Johnny Damon, after 2001, went on to play respectively for the Yankees and the Red Sox, the two most annoying and also wealthiest teams in the American league. In order to replace the star players, Billy Beane, with the help of Jonah Hill (who's character I don't know is fictional or not), crunched a bunch of numbers together to scout out the players that looked bad on paper, but because they statistically got on base a lot more, would be worth buying. This wasn't exactly a feel-good movie about how Beane used a revolutionary new method of scouting and brought a team to victory. Because, let's face it, does anyone remember Oakland winning a World Series any time since 1989? Hell no! Beane is still the GM of the A's and still, they suck big clanking moneyballs. But, the movie isn't about that. Aaron Sorkin, who co-wrote the screenplay, is a genius at getting a different message across. The Social Network wasn't about the invention of Facebook, it was about a nerdy guy who made a lot of complicated choices to become who he was. Moneyball is really about a guy who just tries a different philosophy. When Beane was in high school, the scouts all said he'd be a star player and convinced him to give up a Stanford scholarship to play for the Mets, but he bottomed out. As it's pointed out in Moneyball, this happens all the time. Not even just in baseball, but in most sports. Scouts really don't know jack shit about how a player is going to develop, so why not try this way? It seemed a perfect fit for Beane, who's portrayed by Pitt as a guy who wants badly to not have anything human to do with the players. He didn't want to have to get to know them, less he has to fire or trade them. He'd rather base everything on numbers, let the cold facts make the decisions for him. He struggles with it until he understand that you can't take romance about of baseball. These are human beings, not predictable machines, and Baseball is so ingrained in the American psyche as an escapist pastime that most people aren't going to easily accept something like sabermetrics. I liked Moneyball more than I thought I would. I didn't think there would be any point to basing a movie on something that didn't work. Hey, let's next do a movie on the development of New Coke! But, the theme sold me, and then so did Pitt's performance. Even Jonah Hill was good, not playing the sarcastic fat guy he's known for. I was hoping to see more of Oakland, but I mostly got scenes of that ghetto Coliseum, and all those shipyard structures, but that's just me. I shouldn't have expected Lake Merritt or something. The movie did last a long time so if you're not at all into baseball or the story, you might be looking at your watch.

— the kind that makes spreadsheets and sabermetrics feel as tense as a ninth-inning at-bat. Bennett Miller frames it less like a sports movie and more like a heist film where the score being cased is a full season, and it plays almost like the spiritual predecessor to Ted Lasso: an outsider's unconventional method quietly dismantling an entrenched system. The scene of Jonah Hill walking Brad Pitt through his numbers is the film's clearest thesis statement, and the camera knows it — pushing in tight enough that you can see the pixels on the screen, the data itself becoming the emotional core of the scene. That's the trick of the whole movie: turning cold math into something that comes alive. Pitt and Hill's chemistry does a lot of the heavy lifting too, Billy's practiced confidence playing off Peter's shy, introverted uncertainty in a way that never feels like odd-couple shtick. And Billy Beane's backstory isn't just texture — it's the engine underneath everything, the reason his refusal to accept mediocrity reads as compulsion rather than strategy: a guy who was once the sure thing that didn't pan out, demanding the best from everyone else because he never got to demand it from himself, and never extending that kindness back to the players under him. Even the smaller touches land — the American flag catching the light on the diamond, the surprise of seeing Liverpool's John Henry pop up as a cameo when you already bleed red for that club. There isn't a ton left to say about it at this point except that it's fully earned its status as a cult classic of the genre.

On the surface, this is an underdog story about a baseball team trying to compete with teams that have far more money and resources than they do. But underneath that, it’s such an interesting insight into a side of sport we rarely get to see. The finances, recruitment, statistics and decisions being made behind the scenes are just as important as what eventually happens on the field. What makes it even more interesting watching it now is knowing how much sport has changed since. The kind of data-driven thinking Billy is fighting to introduce has become such a huge part of modern sport, not just baseball. Analytics, finding value in players and trying to gain an advantage through information are now completely normal. You’re basically watching an approach that people thought was ridiculous become part of how modern sport operates. Then there’s Billy himself and the resistance he faces trying to change something that has been done the same way for decades. Everyone around him has their own idea of what a baseball player should look like and how a team should be built, because experience has taught them that’s simply how it works. Billy doesn’t have the money to play by those same rules, so he has to question whether the rules actually make sense in the first place. I really liked that idea. Just because something has always been done a certain way doesn’t mean it’s the best way of doing it. There’s something quite inspiring about watching someone believe in an idea while almost everyone around them is telling them it won’t work. Change means being willing to adapt, evolve and sometimes go against what everyone else accepts as normal. You might not even be the person who ultimately benefits the most from that change, but you can still be the person who proves that another way is possible.

Then you've got Jonah Hill playing a serious role, which is bloody weird to see at first. The craziest part is that this is based on a true story. I know absolutely fuck all about baseball, but even I could appreciate how insane it is that these people were basically trying to change the way the sport was approached by looking at things differently. Sports, but online, using only statistics? “How can you not be romantic about baseball?” That line, delivered by Brad Pitt’s Billy Beane after watching Jeremy Brown trip and stumble back to first base after him hitting a home run, is the moment I keep coming back to every time I watch Moneyball. I gave it five out five stars. I grew up with this story because baseball has been such a huge part of my life, and still is because I’m still playing. I also believe this is Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill’s most underrated and underappreciated work. Both performances carry the film without ever feeling like they’re reaching for attention. It feels very authentic. What I find just as compelling is Billy's relationship with his own scouting team. He gets annoyed at them for judging players purely on the eye test, even though that’s the exact same way he was scouted and brought into the league himself. It’s a strange contradiction, but it’s part of what makes his character work so well for me. Beyond the performances, I think the moneyball movement itself was the most impactful moment in the history of sports. It wasn’t just about analytics changing how teams evaluate players, it was about teaching big organizations across every sport that thinking unconventionally could actually win. That idea is bigger than baseball, and it’s a big part of why this movie has stuck with me for as long as it has.n
